extraction.title: Understanding the symptoms of the common cold and influenza
key_findings: Cytokines and inflammatory mediators are primarily responsible for generating the familiar symptoms of common colds and flu, providing physiological explanations for symptoms previously attributed to folklore.

Systemic URTI symptoms (e.g., fever, headache, myalgia, anorexia) are mainly caused by cytokines released from immune cells, while local symptoms (e.g., sore throat, rhinorrhoea, nasal congestion) are driven by inflammatory mediators like bradykinin and prostaglandins.

Some unpleasant URTI symptoms, such as fever, malaise, and anorexia, are integral to the acute phase response and may aid in recovery from infection, prompting debate on the benefits of their elimination with symptomatic treatments.
Understanding the pathophysiology of URTI symptoms is crucial because most treatments are symptomatic, and clinical trials for new therapies primarily assess changes in symptom scores.
extraction.conclusion: Our understanding of URTI symptoms has improved with the discovery of cytokines and their roles in the acute phase response, providing physiological explanations for symptoms like anorexia previously attributed to folklore. While current URTI treatment focuses on symptom relief, this review suggests that some symptoms, such as fever, malaise, and anorexia, are integral to the acute phase response and may aid recovery. It is debatable whether eliminating these symptoms with non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs is beneficial, and there is currently no evidence that symptomatic treatment interferes with the course of common cold or influenza, an area warranting further research.
